comments.text:
## Failure Mode Handling (added)

### content_hash computation failure
- xxHash fails on file read → treat as stale, rebuild index
- Returns SearchError::HashError with file path context

### Concurrent write race condition
- Process A checks needs_rebuild → false (index valid)
- Process B writes new index simultaneously
- Process A reads stale mmap of old index
- Mitigation: re-validate mtime + content_hash after mmap read; if mismatch, discard and retry

### Stale index mmap retained after file replacement
- Index file deleted and recreated while mmap is open
- OS may still serve old data from page cache
- Mitigation: open with FILE_FLAG_DELETE_ON_CLOSE or re-check file identity (inode + size) post-mmap

### content_hash mismatch on partial read
- File truncated between size check and content read
- Mitigation: verify content_hash matches after full read; if not, treat as stale

### Symbolic link cycles
- .linehash/indexes/ contains symlink pointing outside target directory
- Mitigation: resolve_path() before any file operations; reject if outside .linehash/

### Large file causing OOM on content_hash
- xxHash is streaming but still allocates; very large files (>1GB) could memory pressure
- Mitigation: chunked xxHash; document memory budget in IndexStats

## Edge Cases (added)
- needs_rebuild called on non-existent file → return true (no index exists, will build fresh)
- Index file exists but is 0 bytes → return true (corrupt, rebuild)

title: T2: Design Binary Index Format

comments.author: quangdang46
comments.text:
## WHY This Matters
The binary format determines index file size, read performance, and future upgrade path. Memory-mapped access requires careful alignment and layout.

## WHAT To Do
Design complete binary format in format.md:
```
Header (24 bytes):
  - magic: [0xC7, 0x7R, 0xG, 0xP] (4 bytes)
  - version: u32 LE (4 bytes)
  - flags: u32 LE (4 bytes)
  - line_count: u32 LE (4 bytes)
  - trigram_count: u32 LE (4 bytes)
  - meta_offset: u64 LE (8 bytes)

Lookup Table (trigram_count * 12 bytes):
  - For each trigram (sorted ascending):
    - trigram_key: u32 LE (4 bytes)
    - posting_offset: u64 LE (8 bytes)

Postings Section:
  - For each trigram:
    - posting_count: u32 LE (4 bytes)
    - postings: [posting_count * 6 bytes]

Metadata Section (at meta_offset):
  - file_mtime: u64 LE (8 bytes)
  - file_size: u64 LE (8 bytes)
  - content_hash: u64 LE (8 bytes)
  - magic_end: u64 LE (0xDEADBEEFCAFEBABE)
```

- [ ] All field sizes and offsets are specified

## Failure Mode Handling
- Pattern is empty string → return TrigramQuery::None (no search possible)
- Pattern is just ".*" or ".+" → return TrigramQuery::None (too generic)
- Pattern is just "^" or "$" → return TrigramQuery::None (anchors only)

- Plain literals → extract all trigrams (AND logic)
- Character classes [abc] → extract union of trigrams for each char
- Quantifiers {3,} → handled but may return None if too few trigrams
- Anchors ^$ → ignored for trigram extraction

description:
Reduce 100k String allocations during parsing/read by moving LineRecord content toward shared/zero-copy storage.

Background: profiling attributes a large share of read/load CPU work to creating 100k owned String instances. The plan proposes an incremental owned abstraction such as Arc<str>, Bytes, or Cow-like storage so Document can stay ergonomic without introducing difficult lifetimes everywhere.

Scope: design and implement the smallest safe migration. Audit call sites that mutate LineRecord content, construct Documents, render output, compute hashes, and build indexes. Materialize owned strings only on mutation paths. Avoid lifetime-heavy APIs unless they clearly simplify the codebase.

Investigate Linux kernel-assisted copying for unchanged portions of atomic writes.

Background: even with optimized edit logic, large unchanged file spans may still pass through userspace. ## Failure Mode Handling (added)

### Corrupted index file
- Index file partially written or malformed
- Mitigation: wrap stats() in try-catch; return IndexStats { is_valid: false } with error context

### Mmap read failure on stats
- Memory-map fails (permissions, resource exhaustion)
- Mitigation: return IndexStats { is_valid: false } with error message; don't crash

### Division by zero in avg_postings
- If trigram_count == 0 (empty index), avg_postings = 0.0 to avoid panic
- Guard: if unique_trigrams == 0 → avg = 0.0

### Large index causing stats OOM
- stats() iterates all postings; for very large indexes could be memory-intensive
- Mitigation: compute incrementally; cap at 1M trigram iterations before returning partial

### Stale stats after index rebuild
- Stats computed on old index but file changed since
- Mitigation: stats() should re-validate index before computing (call needs_rebuild internally)

### Stats format mismatches (human vs JSON)
- JSON output uses camelCase, human uses snake_case labels
- Mitigation: explicit format parameter; separate serialization paths

## Edge Cases (added)
- Empty index (line_count=0, trigram_count=0) → stats should return valid object with zeros
- Trigram count huge but postings sparse → avg_postings = postings.len() as f64 / unique_trigrams as f64

title: linehash v1 implementation program
description:
Purpose:

Background / why this matters:
- The project is intentionally conservative: reject stale, ambiguous, or unsafe edits rather than guessing.
- The implementation order matters because many later commands build directly on a few foundational primitives: hashing, document loading, anchor parsing/resolution, output formatting, and atomic writeback.
- The bead graph should make the critical path obvious, while still exposing parallelizable work once the core stabilizes.

Success definition:
- All v1 acceptance criteria in PLAN.md are represented by concrete, actionable issues.
- Dependencies reflect architectural truth rather than convenience.
- Future sessions can understand not only what to do, but why the sequence exists and what invariants must be preserved.

title: Freeze spec invariants and implementation contracts
description:
Purpose:

Key invariants to preserve:
- Hash exact raw line content excluding only newline terminators.
- Preserve newline style and trailing newline status exactly.
- UTF-8 only in v1.
- Canonical anchor display/input model is based on 2-char hashes with optional line qualification.
- Anchor resolution is safety-first: no silent retargeting.
- Mutation commands accept only single logical lines in v1.
- Whole-file load/transform/writeback is acceptable and preferred for simplicity/auditability.

Why this is first:
These choices determine correctness. Everything downstream assumes them.

Done means:
- The codebase structure and all implementation tickets align with the frozen spec.
- Any contradiction discovered during implementation is captured and reconciled explicitly rather than patched over locally.

title: Audit PLAN.md for internal consistency and hidden implementation assumptions
description:
Purpose:
Perform a dedicated spec-audit pass over PLAN.md before implementation begins.

Why this bead was added:
The original graph jumped from "freeze spec" straight into implementation preparation. That risks discovering contradictions too late. A separate audit bead creates an explicit checkpoint for detecting internal inconsistencies, unclear contracts, or accidental overreach while changes are still cheap.

Specific review targets:
- Internal consistency across the scope list, file structure, data model, CLI contract, phases, tests, and acceptance criteria.
- Places where the plan implicitly promises behavior that is not fully represented in the proposed module APIs.
- Places where later command descriptions depend on hidden helper abstractions that are not yet modeled as tasks.

Done means:
- Any contradictions or under-specified behaviors are captured and resolved in beads/comments before implementation starts.
close_reason: Completed spec audit and captured contradictions/hidden abstractions

comments.author: quangdang
comments.text:
Spec audit findings:

1. Hash semantics are internally inconsistent across project docs. README.md and POC.md describe hashing trimmed line content, while PLAN.md, plan-codex.md, and the bead hierarchy require hashing raw line bytes excluding only newline terminators. This must be frozen to raw-content hashing before implementation; otherwise stale-read detection and whitespace-sensitive formats are weakened.

2. V1 scope has drifted substantially. README.md and plan-codex.md describe a deliberately small v1 (read/index/edit/insert/delete + JSON + atomic writes), but PLAN.md declares a much larger v1 including verify/grep/annotate/patch/swap/move/indent/find-block/stats/from-diff/merge-patches/watch/explode/implode plus dry-run, receipts, audit log, and concurrency guards. This is not just elaboration; it changes the delivery shape and should be explicitly justified or reduced in linehash-39q.1.4.

3. Planned layout is inconsistent across planning artifacts. plan-codex.md assumes a simple root src/ layout. plan-claude.md and PLAN.md switch to a workspace with crates/core. Implementation tickets should align to one layout before bootstrapping.

4. plan-claude.md contains a Rust manifest inconsistency: it places [[bin]] in the workspace root Cargo.toml while also describing a workspace-only root with no package. That is not a valid final shape unless the root is also a package. The implementation should follow PLAN.md's later split with the binary declared in crates/core/Cargo.toml instead.

5. Hidden shared abstractions are implied by command specs but not always called out explicitly in planning text: a common mutation pipeline (resolve anchors -> transform in-memory document -> render/write -> emit dry-run/receipt), shared JSON schema stabilization, reusable diff/receipt rendering helpers, and fixture coverage for newline/UTF-8/concurrency edge cases. These should be treated as first-class implementation concerns, not ad hoc per-command logic.

6. Current repository state matters: there is no checked-in Rust workspace or source tree yet, only docs/spec artifacts and beads. So all architecture today is planned architecture, not implemented architecture.

Recommendation from this audit:
- Freeze raw-content hashing as canonical.
- Treat README.md as needing alignment once scope is finalized.
- Use the workspace + crates/core structure from PLAN.md as the canonical code layout.
- Make the minimal shared primitives explicit before command implementation: document loading, hash/index building, anchor parsing/resolution, output schema, writeback, and shared mutation/receipt plumbing.
- Let linehash-39q.1.4 explicitly decide whether the expanded PLAN.md v1 surface is intentional or should be reduced back toward the smaller README/plan-codex shape.

title: Review and lock user-facing CLI/JSON/error contract before implementation
description:
Purpose:
Review the CLI/output contract from the user's perspective and lock down behavior that most affects usability, trust, and agent integration.

Why this bead was added:
The original graph focused mostly on architecture. This task makes user value explicit in plan space: stable JSON schema, helpful error/hint wording, discoverability of commands, output predictability, and consistency across pretty vs JSON paths.

Focus areas:
- Which outputs should be considered stable interfaces for agents.
- Whether any command defaults should be reconsidered for safer or lower-friction use.
- Whether any names, flags, or error wording should change before implementation.
- Whether any command should gain/lose a dependency on output machinery.

Done means:
- A documented UX contract exists in bead comments/notes sufficient to guide implementation decisions without ad hoc tweaks later.
close_reason: Completed UX contract review and documented stable CLI/JSON/error behavior

comments.author: quangdang
comments.text:
UX/CLI contract review:

Stable interfaces to freeze before implementation:
- Treat pretty output for `read`/`index` as human-readable but intentionally stable enough for agent consumption because README and PLAN both position it that way. Avoid decorative noise, timestamps, color, or summary banners in default output.
- Treat JSON output as a strict machine interface. Once implementation starts, field names/order expectations should be snapshot-tested to prevent accidental drift.

Recommended contract decisions:
1. Canonical anchor syntax should remain `N:hh` in displayed output, with bare `hh` accepted only as convenience input. All pretty outputs that identify lines should emit the qualified form so agents can copy/paste unambiguous anchors directly.
2. `read --json` should be the authoritative source for file metadata (`newline`, `trailing_newline`, `mtime`, `mtime_nanos`, `inode`) and line records. Mutation receipts and dry-run JSON should reuse the same field naming style.
3. Helpful error wording is part of the product. Recovery hints should be considered contractually important for: hash-not-found, stale-anchor, stale-file, mixed-newlines, invalid UTF-8/binary, invalid pattern, and unsupported multi-line content.
4. Exit-code behavior should be explicit and consistent: successful read/index/grep-no-match exit 0; verify exits non-zero if any anchor fails; parse/validation/mutation failures exit non-zero everywhere.
5. `grep` and `annotate` should output in the same anchor-prefixed line format as `read` so their output can feed directly into later commands without translation.
6. `--dry-run` should be supported uniformly on every mutation command or not at all; PLAN already assumes uniform support, which is the better UX.
7. `--json` should avoid mixing diagnostic prose with structured payloads. Human hints belong on stderr or in dedicated JSON fields, not interleaved text.

Usability cautions surfaced by review:
- README currently presents a much smaller command surface than PLAN. Once v1 scope is finalized, README must be updated so users are not taught a different mental model than the implementation provides.
- `read --anchor --context`, `stats`, and `verify` are especially valuable for agent workflows because they reduce token waste and preflight risk. If scope must shrink, preserve those before lower-frequency features like explode/implode or watch.
- The Error Hint System section in PLAN is directionally right, but hints should not prescribe external tools too strongly (for example, mixed-newline hints can mention normalization, but the primary action should still be to re-read or fix the file intentionally).

Implementation guidance implied by this review:
- Output formatting should be centralized so every command shares one rendering policy.
- JSON schema stability deserves snapshot coverage from day one.
- Do not let per-command handlers invent bespoke phrasing or output shapes.

title: Map acceptance criteria and invariants to planned test coverage
description:
Purpose:

Why this bead was added:

comments.author: quangdang
comments.text:
Acceptance-criteria to test-coverage mapping:

Foundational invariants -> required unit tests
- Raw-content hashing excluding newline terminators -> hash.rs determinism/formatting tests plus document.rs line-splitting tests that confirm newline bytes are excluded from hashes.
- Preserve newline style and trailing newline state -> document.rs load tests + writeback.rs round-trip tests for LF, CRLF, empty, and no-trailing-newline fixtures.
- UTF-8 only in v1 -> document.rs invalid-UTF8 rejection test; integration test for binary/non-UTF8 input on read.
- Safety-first anchor resolution -> anchor.rs unit tests for unqualified not-found/unique/ambiguous, qualified match/stale, and range validation ordering.
- Single logical line content only -> command-level integration tests for edit/insert rejecting embedded newlines with recovery-oriented error text.
- Whole-file atomic writeback -> writeback.rs failure-path tests and integration tests asserting target file is byte-identical after failed mutations.

Acceptance criteria -> minimum test hooks
- Unique unqualified hash edits intended line -> edit_cli integration fixture with unique short hash.
- Qualified anchor edits only when hash still matches -> edit_cli stale-anchor success/failure pair.
- Ambiguous hashes never silently choose -> anchor.rs ambiguous unit test + edit_cli ambiguity error snapshot.
- Stale anchors never silently choose -> anchor.rs stale unit test + edit_cli stale error snapshot.
- CRLF preserved / no trailing newline preserved -> writeback.rs unit tests + edit_cli integration on dedicated fixtures.
- `read`/`index` stable for agents -> insta snapshots for pretty and JSON output.
- All mutations atomic -> edit/insert/delete/patch integration tests that inject a failing anchor or writeback failure and then byte-compare the file.
- Every user-facing error includes recovery hint -> snapshot/error-form tests covering not-found, stale-anchor, stale-file, mixed-newlines, invalid UTF-8/binary, invalid pattern, multiline unsupported.
- `verify` reports all failures -> verify_cli mixed-success/failure fixture plus JSON schema snapshot.
- `grep`/`annotate` output reusable as anchors -> integration tests asserting anchor-prefixed output shape matches read-format lines.
- `patch` failure leaves file unchanged -> patch_cli test with one bad op in the middle.
- `--expect-mtime` rejects stale files -> concurrency_cli integration tests.
- `read --context --anchor` limits output -> read_cli neighborhood fixture test.
- swap / indent / find-block / from-diff / merge-patches / explode-implode / watch / dry-run / audit-log criteria -> dedicated integration suites already named in PLAN; each should have at least one golden-path case and one safety/failure-path case.

Coverage gaps / planning notes
1. PLAN has broad acceptance criteria for advanced commands, but the minimum fixture matrix should be centralized early: LF, CRLF, no trailing newline, empty file, duplicate-hash fixture, invalid UTF-8/binary fixture, large-file fixture, and concurrency fixture.
2. Error-message stability is itself part of the contract, so snapshot tests should cover both pretty output and stderr forms.
3. If scope is reduced to a core v1, keep traceability for deferred commands rather than deleting it; they can move to a v1.1 test matrix instead.
4. The test harness bead (linehash-39q.2.2) should explicitly own reusable fixture builders and byte-identity assertions because many acceptance criteria depend on exact preservation rather than semantic equality.

Purpose:

comments.author: quangdang
comments.text:
V1 command-surface review:

Recommendation: split the current PLAN surface into a core v1 and a fast-follow v1.1, even if the implementation graph continues to track everything. The user value curve is heavily front-loaded around a smaller safe-editing pipeline.

Highest-value core to preserve in first shipped release:
- read / index
- edit / insert / delete
- verify
- grep / annotate
- patch
- read --anchor --context
- --json
- --expect-mtime / --expect-inode
- --dry-run
- atomic writes
- clear recovery-oriented errors

Why this set is the best first release:
1. It completes the main agent workflow end-to-end: locate -> inspect -> verify -> mutate -> preview -> commit externally.
2. It directly attacks the biggest real failure modes: exact-old-text mismatch, stale reads, ambiguous anchors, and fragile multi-edit sequences.
3. It keeps the mental model coherent: linehash is primarily a safe line-anchored editing tool, not yet a general file-transformation platform.

Good fast-follow candidates after the core lands:
- swap / move / indent
- stats
- receipt / audit-log
- from-diff

Likely defer-to-post-v1 unless a strong implementation case emerges:
- merge-patches (valuable, but niche until patch adoption is proven)
- watch (less central than read/verify/patch; introduces async/platform complexity)
- explode / implode (interesting interoperability idea, but far from the project's main value proposition)
- find-block (useful, but heuristics/ambiguity burden is higher than the core command family)

Framing suggestion:
- Keep the big PLAN as the full roadmap, but explicitly mark a thinner ship target so bootstrap and foundation work do not inherit unnecessary scope pressure.
- If the project intentionally wants the larger surface in v1, say so explicitly in PLAN and README and justify it as an "agent-safe editing platform" rather than the README's current "simplest tool in the suite" framing. Right now those narratives conflict.

Net: the present command list is not equally v1-worthy. The strongest first product is the safe anchor-editing pipeline; the more exotic orchestration and filesystem-projection commands should not block first release value.

title: Implement hash.rs primitives and tests
description:
Implement hash.rs exactly to spec.

Background:
The short hash is the anchor primitive, so determinism and formatting correctness matter more than cleverness. The function must hash exact raw line content and expose a 2-char lowercase hex representation derived from the low byte of xxh32(seed=0).

Key considerations:
- No trimming.
- Empty string is a normal line.
- Keep full-hash vs short-hash logic isolated to make future hash-length expansion straightforward.

Done means:
- Public API matches the plan.
- Unit tests cover determinism, formatting, whitespace sensitivity, and collision helper behavior.
close_reason: Implemented and validated

title: Implement document.rs loading, rendering, and indexing
description:
Implement document.rs and the in-memory Document model.

Background:
Document loading is where file bytes become the authoritative internal model used by every command. This is also where newline style, trailing newline, binary detection, UTF-8 validation, and file metadata are captured.

Key considerations:
- Preserve exact formatting semantics on render.
- Reject mixed newlines and invalid UTF-8 explicitly.
- Empty-file behavior must match the plan exactly.
- Build line records with both full and short hashes.

Done means:
- load/from_str/build_index/render/len/is_empty exist and obey the specified edge cases.
- Unit tests cover LF, CRLF, empty, no trailing newline, whitespace-only lines, invalid UTF-8, binary files, index collisions, and metadata capture.

Key considerations:
- Cover the full set of planned error conditions, even if some are only used later.
- Preserve actionable wording and recovery hints.
- Keep variants structured enough for tests and command-specific formatting.

title: Implement anchor parsing and safety-first resolution
description:
Implement anchor.rs parsing and resolution.

Background:
This module enforces the project's safety model. It must reject ambiguity and staleness conservatively rather than guessing user intent.

Key considerations:
- Normalize uppercase input but keep canonical lowercase display.
- Qualified anchors must validate the current line's hash, not search for a convenient replacement.
- Range anchors are inclusive and must enforce start <= end.
- Bulk resolution should collect failures for verify/patch workflows.

Done means:
- parse_anchor, parse_range, resolve, resolve_range, and resolve_all exist and pass the plan's required unit tests.

title: Implement output formatting for pretty and JSON modes
description:
Implement output.rs for pretty and JSON formatting.

Background:
Output is part of the API surface because agents and tests will consume it directly. Pretty output must remain stable and JSON schemas must remain predictable.

Key considerations:
- Right-aligned line numbers for read output.
- Context neighborhood merging and anchor marking.
- JSON must include file metadata needed by optimistic concurrency.
- Keep formatters separate from business logic to simplify testing.

Done means:

title: Implement atomic writeback and permission preservation
description:
Implement writeback.rs atomic file replacement.

Background:
Atomic writeback is the safety boundary for every mutation. All modifying commands should funnel through this module so partial writes are impossible under normal failure modes.

Key considerations:
- Temp file must be created in the target directory.
- Flush + sync before persist.
- Preserve permissions where supported.
- Keep rendering edge cases correct for zero-byte results and trailing newline preservation.

Done means:
- atomic_write and permission preservation exist.
- Tests verify round-trip behavior, empty writes, same-directory temp creation, and permission preservation behavior.

title: Implement shared document mutation primitives for all write commands
description:
Purpose:
Design and implement the shared in-memory mutation primitives that all mutating commands will reuse.

Why this bead was added:
The first graph let edit/insert/delete land directly, and later patch/swap/move/indent depended on them implicitly. That is workable, but it pushes too much command-specific logic into each command and risks duplicated line-manipulation behavior. A dedicated mutation-engine bead makes the system more coherent for users because commands will behave more consistently and edge-case fixes will apply everywhere.

- Inclusive-range replacement collapsed to one line
- Insert-after-anchor semantics
- Delete-line semantics
- Line renumber/hash recomputation strategy after mutation
- Shared before/after change capture hooks that later support dry-run and receipts

Done means:

- Commands become thin wrappers around shared semantics.

description:

This is the first point where the tool delivers direct agent value. It also exercises the full stack from load -> resolve -> mutate -> atomic rewrite -> render.

read is the primary discovery command. If this command is awkward or unstable, every downstream workflow becomes harder.

Key considerations:
- Full-file output and context mode are distinct UX paths.
- Context neighborhoods around one or more anchors must merge cleanly.
- JSON must include mtime/inode data for later mutation guards.

- Integration + snapshot coverage exists.

These are the minimum operations needed to prove the linehash editing model. They also create the contract future mutation commands will follow.

Key considerations:
- Single-line content only in v1.
- Range edit collapses inclusive range to one new line.
- Preserve newline style and trailing newline.
- All writes route through atomic writeback.

Done means:

- Integration tests cover round-trip behavior and formatting preservation.

title: Implement mtime/inode concurrency guards
description:
Implement optimistic concurrency guard support.

Background:
The plan assumes agents may operate concurrently. mtime/inode guards prevent a mutation from applying to a file that changed after it was read.

Key considerations:
- Capture metadata at read/load time.
- Wire --expect-mtime and --expect-inode into all mutation paths.
- Fail before touching the file.

Done means:

- Foundational mutation commands reject stale files with the expected error.

title: Implement verify command with aggregate resolution reporting

Implement verify as a bulk pre-flight anchor checker.

Background:
verify exists to separate anchor validation from mutation. This is especially valuable in batch or agent workflows where we want a cheap pre-check.

Key considerations:
- Do not short-circuit after the first failure.
- Exit code semantics matter.
- Output should distinguish success, ambiguity, and failure clearly.

title: Implement grep command returning anchors for regex matches

title: Implement annotate command for content-to-anchor lookup

Implement annotate for reverse lookup from content to anchor.

Background:
annotate supports workflows where an agent knows what a line says but not where it lives. It is the content->anchor inverse of read/index.

Key considerations:
- Substring mode first, regex optional via flag.
- --expect-one should turn ambiguity into an error.
- Output should be directly reusable as anchor input to mutation commands.

title: Implement patch transaction engine and command
description:
Implement patch.rs and the patch command for atomic multi-op transactions.

Background:
patch is one of the most important compound features in the entire plan. It converts a sequence of fragile, stateful edits into one snapshot-based transaction.

Key considerations:
- Deserialize and validate the patch file schema.
- Resolve all anchors against one document snapshot before mutating anything.
- Preserve declared op order in-memory.
- If one op fails, nothing is written.

Done means:
- patch can apply a valid multi-op file transaction.
- A stale/ambiguous/not-found op leaves the file byte-identical.
- dry-run and failure indexing semantics are in place or supported cleanly.

title: Implement dry-run previews, receipts, and audit logging

Key considerations:
- Keep dry-run side-effect-free under all circumstances.
- Receipts must capture before/after line content and hashes plus whole-file hashes.
- Audit logging must append only for successful operations.
